The Market That Came Back Under Its Own Roof
A town of nine thousand rebuilt its covered market without selling it. This is what the work looked like.
The market hall in March 2023, three weeks after the collapse. Photograph by Teodor Vantongeren.
On the second Saturday of February 2023, a little after six in the morning, the roof of the covered market in Pellgrave gave way under four days of wet snow. Nobody was hurt, because the fishmonger who usually opened first had overslept. When she arrived, the cast-iron columns were still standing, the glass lantern that had run the length of the hall since 1887 lay across forty-one stalls, and the town had lost the one building where its people met without an appointment.
I grew up two streets from that hall, and I went back expecting a familiar story: a council without money, a developer with a drawing of flats above a food court, and a few years of hoardings. That is not what happened. Three and a half years later the market is open again, it still belongs to the town, and the people who sell cheese and mend shoes in it are the people who did so before.
This essay is an attempt to set down how that was done, as plainly as I can, because the people who did it are tired of being called a miracle. They would much prefer to be called a method, and to have other towns borrow it.
The habit comes first
The first decision was made before the snow had melted, and by the stallholders, not the council. Within a week, thirty-four of the forty-one traders had moved into the car park behind the hall, under tarpaulins lent by a scaffolding firm whose owner’s mother sold eggs there. They called it the Outside Market, and they kept the old opening hours to the minute.
A market is a habit before it is a building. Ilse Marrowby, who has run the haberdashery stall since 1991, told me that her one fear in those weeks was not the cold, or the takings, which fell by a third, but the thought of her regulars learning a different route through town on a Saturday.
“People will forgive you a tarpaulin. They will not forgive you for being closed.”
The council, for its part, did one useful thing quickly. It declined three offers for the site in the first month, each with a polite letter and a drawing of a glass atrium, and it published all three, with the prices, on its website. People could see exactly what the land was worth to somebody else, and who had said no.
Who owns a market?
The harder question was money. The insurers paid for clearing the site and for about a third of a new roof, and the council could not find the rest without closing a library. A sale and leaseback was proposed, twice, by consultants. Both times the answer turned on a document almost nobody had read: the market charter of 1887, which gave the hall to the town on condition that it be used for the sale of provisions and useful goods, forever.
A retired solicitor named Corwin Aldegrave read it. He spent a month in the county archive and came out with the view that the charter forbade selling the hall but not borrowing against its rents, and that it said nothing about who was allowed to lend. That opened the way to the idea that paid for the roof: a community bond, sold in small units to residents and repaid from stall rents over twenty years.
The terms were deliberately dull, and the steering group resisted every suggestion to dress them up with tiers, rewards or naming rights. I have copied the main ones here from the prospectus, which ran to four pages, because the dullness is the point:
Each bond cost 50 crowns, and no household could hold more than two hundred.
Interest was fixed at two per cent a year, paid every November.
Repayment could come only from stall rents, never from local taxes.
Bondholders got no vote and no discount, only their money back.
The hall itself could not be offered as security to anyone.
It raised 1.3 million crowns in eleven weeks, from 2,140 households, in a town of nine thousand people. The largest holding belonged to the bowls club. The smallest, a single bond, was bought by a class of eight-year-olds who had held a cake sale, in the Outside Market, naturally, and who now receive one crown of interest every November.
It would be easy to make this sound warmer than it was. There were two public meetings at which people shouted. Some traders wanted rents frozen for the life of the bond, which would have made repayment impossible, and some residents wanted the hall rebuilt in steel for half the money. Both groups lost the argument, and a few of them still do not speak to the steering group.
Building with what was left
The design brief fitted on one side of paper. Keep the columns. Keep the footprint. Put back a lantern that lets in daylight, and make the roof strong enough for twice the snow that broke the old one. The architects, a two-person practice from the next valley, added a line of their own: every piece of timber should be small enough for two people to carry, so that local joiners could bid for the work.
Joiners from three local workshops raising the fourth roof truss, May 2024. Photograph by Teodor Vantongeren.
That last line shaped everything. Instead of a few huge glued beams delivered by crane, the new roof is made of 3,600 short lengths of larch, pegged and bolted into lattice trusses in a disused bus depot and then walked, literally walked, down the high street on market days. A roof that arrives in pieces small enough to recognise is a roof that a town feels it has made.
The salvage was just as deliberate. Volunteers spent the summer of 2023 sorting the wreckage into what could be reused, what could be recast and what was simply rubble. About a fifth of the original glass survived and now fills the north gable, slightly green and full of bubbles. The broken ironwork was melted down and poured into new gutter brackets by a foundry forty kilometres away.
When I asked the site manager, Bettina Oskarsdal, what order things had to happen in on a site like this, she counted the stages off on the fingers of one hand, and I wrote them down that same evening, because nobody else seemed to have done so:
Make the columns safe, then test every one of them under load.
Build the trusses indoors through the winter, while the ground was too wet for anything else.
Raise the roof from the south end northwards, one bay a fortnight, so that stalls could move back in behind it.
Glaze the lantern last, in summer, when a dropped pane would land on an empty floor.
The third stage is the one visitors remember. For most of a year the hall was half building site and half market, with a plywood wall on wheels between the two that moved north every other Monday. The fishmonger was the first trader back under cover, in bay one, fourteen months before the last pane went in.
The notice that hung on that moving wall has since been framed and put up beside the east door, where the queue for the bakery passes it. It is the nearest thing the project has to a monument, and it reads, in full:
PELLGRAVE MARKET HALL Open as usual, Tuesday to Saturday, 7 till 3 Stalls 1 to 12 are behind you, under the new roof Stalls 13 to 41 are in the car park, under the old sky This wall moves north every other Monday Mind the joiners
What the first winter taught us
The hall reopened fully on 4 October 2025, and its first winter was a hard one, as if to settle the question. In January the roof carried more snow than had brought down its predecessor. Half the town, by Bettina’s estimate, found a reason to walk past and look up. Nothing moved, except one gutter bracket that had been cast with a flaw and was replaced, by the same foundry, without charge.
Other lessons were less photogenic. The new roof is higher, and the hall is colder than it used to be; the traders along the west wall have asked for doors that close, and they are right. Rents went up by nine per cent to service the bond, and two stallholders who had worked through both winters in the car park decided they could not stay. One now sells from a van outside the east door, which is either a failure of the scheme or a sign that it has edges, depending on whom you ask.
And the bond has to be repaid for another nineteen years, by people who have not yet taken a stall. The steering group, which has turned itself into a small trust with elected seats for traders and bondholders, posts its accounts on a board by the scales every quarter. So far the rents cover the interest with a little to spare. Nobody pretends that will be true every year.
What I keep returning to is how little of this depended on anyone being unusually generous or unusually clever. It depended on a few specific refusals: to sell, to close, to build something that only a crane could assemble. Each refusal made the next step slower and dearer than the alternative, and each one kept the hall in the hands of people who would be standing in it on a wet Tuesday in March.
If you live in a town with a broken building and a drawer full of developers’ letters, the trust will send you its prospectus, its charter opinion and its truss drawings, free. Write to the market office; they answer slowly, because the office is one desk behind the cheese stall. And if you are passing through Pellgrave on a Saturday, go in by the north door a little before noon, when the light comes through the old green glass, and buy something small from somebody who was there.
